summary: Describes an OSPF extension to reduce periodic flooding of Link State Advertisements in stable networks. Normally OSPF refreshes most LSAs every 30 minutes, and this document proposes making wider use of DoNotAge LSAs to cut that protocol traffic. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A town crier shouts the same news every half hour even if nothing changed. This memo says that if nothing is changing, routers can stay quiet and save everyone the noise.

questions: how often does ospf refresh lsas
subtitle: Lets OSPF routers stop re-flooding unchanged LSAs every 30 minutes by using DoNotAge LSAs more widely.

tldr.problem: OSPF requires every LSA to be refreshed every 1800 seconds or it expires at 3600 seconds, so even stable networks carry steady protocol traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Flooding-reduction-capable routers flood their self-originated LSAs with the DoNotAge bit set, so the re-flooding interval can stretch to a configured forced-flooding interval while real changes are still flooded at once.
tldr.outcome: Protocol overhead drops in stable topologies. The feature is off by default and builds on the demand circuit extensions.

today: RFC 4136 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Refresh Problem
sections.content:
Large OSPF networks see non-negligible protocol traffic even when their topology is stable. OSPF requires every Link State Advertisement (LSA) to be refreshed every 1800 seconds, or it expires on reaching 3600 seconds. Only DoNotAge LSAs are exempt.

This memo proposes generalizing the use of DoNotAge LSAs so that the expiry no longer forces periodic re-flooding.
sections.eli5: Routers keep repeating old news on a timer, even in a quiet network. This idea stops the repeats.

sections.title: How Flooding Reduction Works
sections.content:
The enhancement relies on the DoNotAge bit and the Indication-LSA specified in RFC 1793, the demand circuit extensions. Capable routers keep sending hellos and keep aging their own LSAs in their database, but they flood self-originated LSAs with the DoNotAge bit set. These LSAs need not be re-flooded every 30 minutes, and the interval can stretch to the configured forced-flooding interval.

A change in an LSA's contents still causes a reoriginated LSA to be flooded immediately with the bit set. Received LSAs from other routers that carry the DoNotAge bit are flooded on normal or flooding-reduction-only interfaces within the LSA's flooding scope. On an interface that is both flooding-reduction-capable and Demand-Circuit, flooding happens only if the contents changed.
sections.eli5: Routers still say hello to their neighbours, but they only repeat the news on a slower schedule, and they announce changes right away.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Routers that support the demand circuit extensions can process DoNotAge LSAs from flooding-reduction routers. They suppress flooding of DoNotAge LSAs on demand circuit interfaces but flood them on other interfaces.

If some routers in the routing domain, stub area or NSSA area lack those extensions, the feature is subject to the demand circuit interoperability constraints in section 2.5 of RFC 1793. Detecting an LSA with the DC bit clear causes self-originated DoNotAge LSAs to be reoriginated with the bit clear, and non-self-originated DoNotAge LSAs to be purged.
sections.eli5: Older routers can still understand the quiet routers, and if one cannot, everyone goes back to the old chatty way.

sections.title: Configuration and Security
sections.content:
The feature must be enabled by configuration and is off by default. flooding-reduction turns it on for all interfaces or a listed subset. flooding-interval sets the minutes between periodic floods of self-originated LSAs: the default and minimum are both 30 minutes, and a value of infinity prevents re-flooding of unchanged LSAs.

The memo says it creates no new security issues for OSPF. Security for base OSPF is covered in RFC 2328.
sections.eli5: There is a switch, off by default, and a timer that says how rarely to repeat old news.
